title: TaxGPT vs Juno: Prep Automation or a Full AI Tax OS?
summary: TaxGPT vs Juno: compare AI tax prep automation, planning, research, and return review to determine which platform fits your firm's workflow.
body_markdown:
## What Each Platform Is Built to Do


Every tool in this category sits somewhere between a point tool and an operating system. A point tool is built to do one job in the pipeline exceptionally well. An operating system is built to run the whole pipeline. Neither is a better category to be in. They're solving for different problems, and the right fit depends on which stage of the workflow is actually your bottleneck.


### Juno: purpose-built for the prep stage


Juno does one job and does it well: get client documents into your tax software with as little manual typing as possible. It reads W-2s, 1099s, K-1s, balance sheets, and 92+ other document types, then maps every extracted figure back to its source with bounding boxes, so a reviewer can check a number in seconds instead of hunting through a PDF.


The workflow is a clean three steps. Documents come in, Juno builds workpapers your team can mark up together, then the verified data pushes straight into Drake, Lacerte, ProConnect, or CCH Axcess. No re-keying, no export files. Beyond the tax software itself, Juno connects broadly into the tools firms already run day to day: TaxDome, Karbon, Canopy, SmartVault, Box, QuickBooks Online, Xero.


Pricing is transparent by design. One flat rate per return, whether it's a simple W-2 filing or a 40-page partnership return with six K-1s. No complexity surcharges, no enterprise sales call required to find out what something costs.


### TaxGPT: built to run the whole pipeline


TaxGPT starts from a different premise: prep is one stage of a much longer workflow, and the stages around it (research, review, client communication, client history) are where firms lose just as much time. So TaxGPT is built as an AI Operating System, not a single tool bolted onto one step.


Research runs on a full US and Canada engine with cited answers to the code and treasury regulations. Prep automation runs through Cowork, agents that operate inside your existing tax software the same way Juno does, across 1040, 1065, 1120, and 1120-S. Once a return is complete, Agent Andrew reviews it for errors, missed deductions, and audit risk. TaxGPT Writer drafts the client memos, emails, and IRS notice responses that come out of that work. Client Intelligence keeps a running record of each client's history, structure, and prior positions, so nothing gets re-explained from scratch every filing season.


That's the difference worth sitting with. Juno automates one stage of the pipeline extremely well. TaxGPT automates the pipeline.


## Prep Automation Head-to-Head


This is the one place where TaxGPT and Juno are doing genuinely comparable work, and it deserves a straight, precise comparison rather than a category argument dressed up as one.


**The philosophical difference:** Juno extracts and structures data, then pushes the finished result into your tax software. Cowork's AI Tax Preparation agents log into your tax software and operate it directly. Same tools on the other end, Drake, Lacerte, ProConnect, CCH Axcess, but the two platforms sit on different sides of that software's login screen.


**How Juno's version works:** Juno reads source documents, builds a workpaper binder your team can mark up together, and once everything is verified, pushes the data into fields in your tax software. The preparer, or the software itself via API, is still the one entering it. Every figure links back to its source document with a bounding box, so a reviewer can confirm any number in seconds. The human touches the binder review, then the push is largely mechanical.


**How Cowork's version works:** The Tax Prep Agent opens the tax software the same way a preparer does, reads workpapers, enters data, runs diagnostics, and prepares the return inside the platform itself. No export step, because there's nothing to export. TaxGPT's own materials are explicit about what stays fixed here: agents autonomously log into and operate your existing tax and practice management software without migration or new tools to learn, and every workflow surfaces a full audit trail while keeping licensed professionals in the review seat, not the execution seat. When prep is complete, it hands off to Agent Andrew, which reconciles the finished return against source documents and flags audit-sensitive items for sign-off, so the human's first real touchpoint is a completed return with exceptions already surfaced, not a workpaper binder mid-build.


**Where exceptions surface, concretely:** With Juno, discrepancies show up during the binder review, before the return exists in the tax software. With Cowork, discrepancies show up after the return exists, as flags on the finished product, since the agent has already carried the workflow through to a prepared return.


**What this means for review capacity:** TaxGPT's own reported numbers here are worth stating plainly rather than dressing up: firms using AI-prepared returns report reviewers handling roughly three times the volume, and a 25-person firm preparing 5,000 returns a season saw a 28% capacity increase within 60 days, without adding headcount. That's a different kind of gain than time saved on data entry. It's a shift in what the reviewer's job looks like at the start of their day.


**What's true and worth conceding:** if a firm's only bottleneck is data entry, and the process around it, who reviews, how workpapers get assigned, how the finished return gets delivered, is working fine as is, Juno is a smaller, more contained change. It slots into an existing workflow without asking a firm to rethink where the human sits in the process. That's a real advantage for a firm that isn't looking to restructure how prep happens, just to stop typing the numbers by hand. Cowork asks more of a firm on day one, because it's not just faster data entry, it's a different point in the workflow where a human first looks at the return.


## Everything Around the Return: Research, Review, Drafting, Client Context


Prep is one stage in a return's life. Everything before it and after it is where the real gap sits. Juno reaches into part of this with prep-stage review and AI planning suggestions, but not into cited research, full post-prep return review, drafting, or persistent client memory.


### Research


Juno has no research capability. A partnership return hits a Section 704(b) allocation question, and the preparer is on their own to answer it before the return can move forward. That's one of the[common tax research challenges](https://www.taxgpt.com/taxgpt-insights/tax-research-challenges) firms run into once data entry stops being the bottleneck.


[AI tax research](https://www.taxgpt.com/ai-tax-research) through TaxGPT covers US federal, state, local, and territorial law plus Canadian federal and provincial law, with citations to the IRC, Treasury Regulations, and rulings on every answer. A question that took 30 to 60 minutes now takes seconds.


### Review


Juno's Reviewer is prep-stage QA: it catches transcription errors and mismatches between source docs and what got entered. Agent Andrew reviews the completed return for audit risk and missed savings, not just data-entry accuracy, flagging red (errors), green (missed savings), and cleared items. Most Agent Andrew reviews finish in 5 to 10 minutes, against 30 to 90 minutes for a manual senior-level review. See the full[manual review vs AI return review](https://www.taxgpt.com/taxgpt-insights/manual-tax-review-vs-agent-andrew) breakdown for how the two compare stage by stage.


### Drafting


Juno has no client-communication drafting; it doesn't produce memos, emails, or IRS notice responses. Writer drafts client memos, emails, and IRS notice responses (CP2000, CP14, CP504, CP503) in the same platform where the research and return already live.


### Client context


Juno compares against prior-year data during prep but keeps no persistent, cross-engagement client profile, so context isn't carried forward the way Client Intelligence does. Client Intelligence keeps a running record of history, entity structure, and prior positions, so next April doesn't start from scratch.


### The math


Research: 30–60 minutes down to seconds. Review: 30–90 minutes down to 5–10. Reviewers handling AI-prepared returns report roughly 3x the volume. Juno's 50% cut in prep time is real. It's one stage of a pipeline that, for most firms, doesn't end when the data entry does.


## Pricing and How to Think About Cost


Juno charges a per-return rate on a volume slider, so the cost drops as your return count rises, with higher-volume firms moving to custom enterprise pricing. That model is easy to forecast: estimate your return count and you have a rough number. TaxGPT prices the platform through a demo, because it covers several functions at once rather than a single per-unit output.


Easy to forecast is not the same as cheapest to run, though, and this is where a per-return number can mislead. Per-return pricing scales with every return you file, every season, and it pays for one job: data entry. A firm that also needs research, review, and client-communication drafting ends up buying and billing several point tools to cover the ground one platform does. So the honest comparison isn't Juno's per-return rate against a TaxGPT seat; it's Juno plus a research tool plus a review tool against TaxGPT alone.


**Why the comparison isn't apples to apples** . A per-return tool is straightforward to model: multiply cost per return by return volume, done. A platform is pricing something with more moving parts, hours saved on research, review, drafting, and client communication, so the ROI math has more inputs but also more places value shows up. TaxGPT publishes an[ROI framework](https://www.taxgpt.com/taxgpt-insights/taxgpt-roi) built around exactly this, time saved across research, accuracy, and client service rather than a single per-unit cost, and offers an ROI calculator through the same page for firms that want to run their own numbers.


What to actually ask in each demo, instead of guessing at a number:


- **For Juno:** At your firm's return mix and volume, where does the per-return rate land, and does that number hold if your business-return share grows next season?
- **For TaxGPT:** What does a seat actually include at your firm's size, and how does the platform price change as you add Cowork workflows beyond prep?
- **For both:** What's the realistic payback period once you count hours saved across every function you'd actually use, not just the one that first got you looking?


The honest takeaway: pricing opacity here isn't a red flag on either side. It's a reason to walk into both demos with your own volume and workflow numbers ready, rather than trying to compare two published rate cards that don't exist.


## Which Should Your Firm Choose?


**Choose Juno if:**


- Your bottleneck is data entry and workpapers, full stop, not cited research or post-prep return review.
- You want your existing tax-software process left untouched, with a tool that plugs into the step you already have rather than changing how the step works.
- Per-return pricing fits how you think about cost. You'd rather pay by volume than by seat.
- You're already running TaxDome or Karbon for practice management and want something that slots into that stack without adding a new system of record.


**Choose TaxGPT if:**


- The constraint isn't one stage, it's the whole pipeline: research, prep, review, and client communication all eating time, not just data entry.
- You'd rather run one platform than stitch together a stack of point tools, each with its own login, billing, and support relationship.
- You need Canadian coverage alongside US federal, state, local, and territorial research. Juno doesn't offer this at all.
- Attested security matters to your engagement letters or your firm's own risk policy. TaxGPT is SOC 2 Type II; Juno states it's SOC 2 certified without specifying which type.


Neither of these is a hedge. A firm whose only real problem is typing numbers off a W-2 doesn't need an operating system, and buying one anyway just means paying for capability nobody on staff will touch. A firm losing hours to research and review every week isn't going to fix that with a faster data-entry tool, no matter how good the extraction is.


**The trial-week test**


Don't decide from a table. Run the same three returns through both platforms and score them side by side, one straightforward 1040, one with a K-1 or multi-state wrinkle, one business return.


1. **Data-entry time.** Use Juno's 5 free preparations against a TaxGPT demo on the same returns. Time how long each takes from source document to a workpaper or draft return ready for review.
2. **Exception quality.** What did each tool actually flag, a transcription mismatch, a missing form, an audit-risk item, a missed deduction? Note not just how many flags, but what kind.
3. **Review findings.** Run Agent Andrew against Juno's Reviewer on the same completed return. Did one catch something the other didn't?
4. **What's still manual?** After each tool has done its part, what's left for a human to actually do? The research question that still needs answering. The memo that still needs writing. The client email that still needs drafting from scratch.


That last line is usually the one that settles it. If the answer is "basically nothing else," Juno's doing its job well and there's no reason to pay for more. If the answer is "a lot," that's the pipeline TaxGPT is built to close.


### FAQ


#### Q: Does Juno do tax research?


No. Juno is built for the prep pipeline, extraction, workpapers, and pushing data into your tax software, and doesn't include a research function. If a return raises a question that needs a cited answer (a position under Section 704(b), a cost-basis call on a foreign sale), that still has to be resolved outside the platform. TaxGPT Research covers that gap directly, with cited answers across US federal, state, local, and territorial law plus Canada.


#### Q: What’s the difference between TaxGPT and Juno?


Juno is a prep-workflow point tool: it extracts data from source documents and pushes it into your tax software, covering 1040s, 1065s, 1120s, and 1120-S returns. TaxGPT is an AI Operating System where prep automation is one capability among several, alongside research, return review, drafting, and client intelligence. The two overlap on prep. TaxGPT covers everything around it that Juno doesn't touch.


#### Q: Does Juno review tax returns?


Yes, but at a different stage than Agent Andrew. Juno's Reviewer compares source documents against the return as it's being prepared, flagging mismatches like a W-2 wage that doesn't match the 1040, a missed state filing, or a K-1 that shifted from the prior year, plus firm-defined custom checks. It's built to catch data-entry and transcription errors before sign-off. Agent Andrew reviews the completed return itself for audit risk and missed tax-saving opportunities, a judgment layer on top of a finished product rather than a check on data entry. Firms sometimes use both: Reviewer during prep, Agent Andrew after.
